title: LTS-aware traffic lease controller for deterministic stage gates and rapid rollback
creator: Ava Chen
description: Problem statement: Hosted API rollouts across regions and LTS channels currently rely on timed windows and soft checks. This leads to non-deterministic cutovers, delayed rollbacks when telemetry degrades, and edge cases where staged traffic is accepted before downstream caches/kv-shards are warmed. Proposal: implement a lease-based Traffic Lease Controller (TLC) that gates traffic shifts with deterministic ownership, TTL-protected leases, and telemetry-integrated acceptance criteria. The TLC will be LTS-aware (so stable LTS channels can opt for stricter acceptance rules), integrate with existing rollout gating service, and emit structured events used by Console runbooks and automated rollback operators.
acceptance_criteria: 1) TLC issues a time-bound lease for a target region+version before shifting >0% traffic. 2) Traffic shift proceeds only after defined telemetry predicates (latency, error-rate, p99 tails, downstream cache hit-rate) evaluate green for the lease warmup window. 3) If predicates fail during warmup or within lease TTL, TLC retracts the lease and triggers automated rollback/fallback policy. 4) Operator can pin an LTS channel to bypass non-essential warmup predicates for critical fixes. 5) All lease state and decisions are emitted to event stream and visible in Console with per-route trace links.
implementation_notes:
- Controller is an independent service with a small in-memory authoritative lease store and optional durability backed by dynamo/replicated kv for cross-region recovery.
- Leases have deterministic TTLs and monotonic epoch numbers to prevent split-brain during concurrent rollouts.
- TLC exposes an admission webhook used by the routing plane to accept/reject traffic shifts.
- Telemetry predicates are configurable per LTS channel and per-customer tier; default predicates live in rollout policies.
- Fallbacks: if the telemetry service is degraded, TLC can operate in a conservative mode (deny new leases) or in a permissive mode under operator override.
- Security: leases are signed with the controller key; Console and operators validate signatures before performing any manual cutover.
tradeoffs_and_risks:
- Adding a centralized lease controller increases an operational surface and needs high availability; mitigated by small state and multi-region replication.
- Conservative gating improves reliability but increases time-to-ship for routine rollouts; we mitigate with per-LTS policy tuning and an operator bypass for critical security fixes.
- Integration with telemetry increases coupling between metrics pipeline and deployments; mitigation: define minimal viable predicates and clear fallback modes.
- Potential for lease contention during overlapping rollouts; design uses epoch last-writer-wins semantics plus explicit operator holdpoints to resolve conflicts.
qa_plan: 1) Unit tests for lease lifecycle and predicate evaluation. 2) Integration tests that simulate canary failure modes and assert rollback triggers. 3) Staging canary: deploy TLC in a staging region and perform synthetic rollouts to validate warmup gating and console visibility. 4) Chaos test: inject telemetry delays/failure and observe modes (conservative/permissive).
rollout_plan: Phase 1: Canary in eu-west-1 with internal traffic only; verify metrics and rollback behavior (2 weeks). Phase 2: Progressive enablement for non-critical LTS channels across three regions using 5%, 25%, 100% step strategy with 15m warmup windows. Phase 3: Default enablement for all LTS channels with operator training and runbook. Manual operator bypass available as emergency button behind SSO+2FA.
